fields.meta_title: Employee Availability Form That Checks Shifts | Emergent
fields.meta_description: What goes on an employee availability form, how to fill out hours, and an app that checks every draft schedule against the hours staff can work.
fields.h1: Build an Employee Availability Form That Checks Every Shift
fields.hero_description: An employee availability form records the days and hours each person can work. Describe how you schedule, and Emergent builds the form plus the shift checks that read from it.
fields.features_heading: Availability That Stays Attached to the Schedule
fields.features_subheading: A printed availability sheet gets filed away. Emergent's version keeps each person's hours and checks them when shifts go out.
fields.feature_1:
Weekly hours saved per employee

Stores each employee's open hours by weekday, with a start and end time for every window. Managers see the whole team's grid in one view, sorted by role or by location.
fields.feature_2:
Draft schedules checked before publish

Compares every shift in a draft against the hours that person said they can work. A shift that starts early or runs late is flagged for the manager before the team sees it.
fields.feature_3:
Hour caps for workers under 16

Holds employees aged 14 and 15 to the federal school-week hour limits, and ends their evening windows at 7 p.m. outside summer. Older staff keep the hours they entered.
fields.feature_4:
Changes with an effective date

Accepts new hours that start on a date the employee picks. Sends the manager a Slack message with approve and decline buttons, then rechecks every shift booked past that date.
fields.feature_5:
Seasonal availability surveys

Sends one availability request to the team before a holiday rush or summer break. Answers fill a dashboard that counts available people per day against the headcount you need.
fields.feature_6:
Source code in your GitHub repo

Exports the full codebase to your GitHub repository. Engineers can connect saved availability to a scheduling or payroll tool's API, or ask Emergent to add that sync in one prompt.

fields.tab_content_1:
One Saturday shift flagged out of 14

Kitchens schedule a week at a time. Marcus Bell, a line cook, can work Saturdays only after 4 p.m., and his form says so. The manager's draft puts him on an 11 a.m. Saturday shift anyway. Of the 14 shifts on that week's schedule, the app flags this one as outside his availability before the schedule is published.
fields.tab_content_2:
A 15-year-old's week, held to 18 hours

Federal rules treat a 15-year-old differently. Ava Brooks, a host, marks every weekday open until 9 p.m. During the school year she can work three hours on a school day and nothing after 7 p.m. The form trims each weekday window to 4 p.m. until 7 p.m. and caps her school week at 18 hours.
fields.tab_content_3:
Approved in Slack two weeks before classes start

Availability rarely stays put. Nina Ortiz, a barista, starts evening classes in 14 days and blocks Tuesday and Thursday after 3 p.m. from that date on. Her manager approves the change in Slack. Two shifts already booked past the start date no longer fit, and both go back on the schedule as open shifts.
fields.tab_content_4:
Who can work Dec 24, counted against the need

December is where a team's availability gets tested. A store sends one holiday survey to its 24 staff, and every answer lands in a dashboard. Each day is counted against a need of 8 people on the floor. Dec 24 has 5 people available, 3 short, and the store manager gets an alert before the schedule is drafted.

fields.howto_title: How to Make an Employee Availability Form
fields.howto_description: An availability form is only as useful as the schedule it feeds. These seven steps start with how you schedule and end with a record you can point to later.
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick the unit you schedule in: hour windows or fixed shifts. A restaurant with split shifts needs hour windows. A warehouse running set shifts only needs to know which ones each person can take, and a checkbox per shift does the job.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Lay out the seven days and give each one two time boxes, plus an unavailable option. A grid is faster to fill in than a free-text box, and it gives the schedule something concrete to check each shift against.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask for the hours someone can work and, separately, the hours they prefer to work. Managers fill the schedule from the first set and use the second to decide who gets a shift when two people qualify for it.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Include a field for the most hours a person wants each week. Students and people with a second job often cap their own hours. A schedule that ignores the cap tends to come back as a stack of swap requests by Wednesday.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Collect date of birth for anyone under 18 and apply the federal hour limits to 14- and 15-year-olds. Check your state labor department's rules for minors as well before you set the caps, and apply whichever is stricter.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Let employees update their hours with a start date instead of overwriting the old answer. Set the notice you need, such as two weeks, and route each change to the manager who builds that team's schedule for approval.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Store every past version with the date it changed and who approved it. When someone disputes a shift they say they could never work, the record shows what their availability said during that exact week.

plan.angle: The live SERP is printable PDFs, Etsy grids and generic form-builder templates that collect a week of open hours and stop there; nobody checks the grid against the schedule, the hour rules for a 15-year-old or a change that lands mid-month. This page answers what goes on the form and how to fill it out, then builds the part a template cannot: availability saved per employee and checked every time a manager drafts a schedule.
